subject: Banking
title: First Republic Bank: The Wealth Bank
description: A quick, practical guide to First Republic Bank: The Wealth Bank.

hook.text: First Republic catered to wealthy clients in San Francisco and New York.

buildup.text: First Republic offered jumbo mortgages at below-market rates to attract wealthy depositors.

discovery.text: When SVB failed, wealthy depositors panicked and pulled $100 billion from First Republic despite reassurances.

twist.text: 11 major banks deposited $30 billion to rescue First Republic. It wasn't enough.

climax.text: First Republic proved that even serving the wealthy doesn't prevent bank runs.

punchline.text: Served the wealthy. Lost $100 billion in deposits.

quiz.question: What happened to the $30 billion rescue deposit for First Republic?
options: It wasn't enough, and JPMorgan acquired the bank anyway

details.summary: First Republic Bank catered to wealthy clients with below-market mortgage rates and exceptional service. When interest rates rose sharply, its portfolio of cheap mortgages lost value and wealthy depositors fled, leading to its seizure and sale to JPMorgan.
details.whyItMatters: First Republic's failure showed that even a well-run bank serving wealthy clients can be destroyed by interest rate risk. Its business model of cheap mortgages for rich clients became a liability overnight.
takeaways: First Republic offered mortgages at rates well below market to attract wealthy clients
Rising rates made its low-rate mortgage portfolio worth billions less than face value
JPMorgan acquired the failed bank's assets in an FDIC-brokered deal

faq.question: Why did a bank serving wealthy clients fail?
faq.answer: First Republic's strategy of offering below-market mortgages meant its assets lost massive value when rates rose. Wealthy clients had deposits far exceeding FDIC limits, so they quickly moved money to perceived safer institutions after SVB's failure.

faq.question: How did JPMorgan benefit from First Republic's failure?
faq.answer: JPMorgan acquired First Republic's assets at a significant discount with FDIC loss-sharing agreements. The deal added wealthy clients and a premium brand to JPMorgan's portfolio while the FDIC absorbed estimated losses of $13 billion.
